approvedAsIs.name: Shagbark hickory nut
reasons: The one deadly lookalike for a nut picked up off the ground in eastern woods — buckeye / horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum, glabra, flava, pavia) — is present, flagged 'deadly', and its tell works on the part actually harvested: the seed in hand is smooth, glossy mahogany with one broad pale hilum scar, has no bony shell, and cuts to one solid ivory mass, versus the 4-angled whitish-tan bony shell and partitioned lobed halves of Carya. That is a nut-level tell, not a flower- or leaf-only tell, so it still works in late November after leaf drop; the opposite/palmate vs alternate/pinnate tree check is correctly offered as a secondary confirmation, not the primary one. The entry also correctly notes the Aesculus capsule is 3-valved (not 4) and that spininess proves nothing since flava and pavia capsules are smooth.
caution 'expert' is correct and consistent with the schema definition — a deadly lookalike (Aesculus) is listed.

No deadly lookalike appears to be missing. The other realistic confusions in range are all covered or benign: bitternut (sulfur-yellow valvate buds, tight bark, thin husk splitting only from the middle to the tip — bitter, correctly 'unpalatable', not toxic), pignut (pear-shaped, thin clinging husk, round unridged nut, shaggy-topped but attached ridges — correctly 'unpalatable'), and shellbark (C. laciniosa) is explicitly named inside the bitternut tell as the other genuinely shaggy 4-valved species, which is edible and better, so no risk from that overlap. Poison ivy as a climbing vine on the trunk is a genuinely useful contact-hazard inclusion given the entry tells you to look at and handle shaggy bark, and it is correctly rated 'toxic' with the burning/dead-vine warning.

The bark tell is honest about its own failure mode — it states outright that young shagbarks are NOT shaggy and routes you to the leaf (5, sometimes 7 leaflets, terminal three largest, ciliate teeth), which is the right correction for the season when a beginner is under a non-shaggy tree.

Required preparation is right and specific: hickory needs no leaching (correctly contrasted with acorns so a beginner does not conflate the two), there is a concrete post-crack positive check, drying is given a duration (a week or two, single layer) with refrigerate/freeze after because the kernel is oily and goes rancid, mouldy/dark/shrivelled kernels are to be discarded, and insect control is a specific action with a duration (freeze a couple of days) plus concrete reject criteria (rattles, floats, small round exit hole). The tree-nut cross-reactivity warning for pecan/walnut allergy is present and correctly framed as potentially anaphylactic.
months [8,9,10] = September, October, November, which matches the stated drop window and the text 'September into November'. Schema-valid 0-indexed.

Schema compliance is exact: all required fields present, no extra fields, caution is one of the three allowed values, all four lookalike danger values are legal, months are integers 0-11, regions and terrain values are all from the allowed sets, and lookalikes each have exactly name/danger/tell. Ten sources, all extension-service, USDA, state agency or poison-center.

NON-BLOCKING GAP: 'southcentral' is missing from regions even though the habitat text explicitly extends the range to eastern Texas and eastern Oklahoma, and southcentral is defined as exactly {TX, OK} in src/data/seasonal-regional.ts. This is under-inclusive — an eastern Texas or Oklahoma forager simply will not be shown the entry — so it hides the species rather than sending anyone to the wrong place. Worth adding, but not a safety block. (Arkansas and Louisiana are already covered because this codebase files them under southeast.)

NON-BLOCKING NIT: terrain 'upland' is documented as 'dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub', while this entry describes fertile, often north/east-facing mesic upland slopes; and the habitat text notes that in Arkansas, Mississippi and Louisiana it is chiefly a river-bottom tree, which argues for adding 'wetland' (floodplain) for the southern part of the range. Both are coverage/labelling imprecision, not misdirection.

approvedAsIs.name: Acorns (white oak group)
reasons: APPROVE. Entry is at /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/foraging-research/corrected-pass1.json (index 16 of 18). No blocking safety defect found: the deadly lookalike is present and correctly rated, the tells work on the part and in the season actually harvested, and the mandatory leaching step carries specific durations and endpoint tests.

Deadly-lookalike coverage is complete for this harvest. The realistic hazard for someone picking nuts off the ground under a tree in Aug-Nov is Aesculus, and both branches are covered: horse chestnut (A. hippocastanum) as 'deadly' and native buckeyes (A. glabra, flava, pavia, californica) as 'toxic', with California buckeye called out by name as the specific West-coast trap in blue oak / valley oak woodland. Red-oak-group acorns are correctly rated 'unpalatable', not toxic. I could not identify a further deadly or seriously toxic confusable: nothing else in US oak woodland drops an acorn-like nut, and Castanea/Notholithocarpus (chestnut, tanoak) are edible.
caution: 'expert' is correct and matches the schema rule, since a lookalike is rated 'deadly'.

The horse chestnut tell is decisive and, critically, it works on the harvested part itself rather than only on the tree. It leads by explicitly discarding the unreliable discriminator ('Ignore size - it proves nothing, because bur oak acorns run to about 1.5 in'), then gives nut anatomy that holds year-round on a nut lying on pavement: acorn = pointed apex (dried style) + small basal cap scar + dull striped shell; Aesculus = no apex point + one broad matte pale hilum over a third of one face + glossy mahogany. The overhead backup (alternate simple vs opposite palmately compound; scaly cup vs prickly leathery capsule) is a genuine second independent check. This does not fail in November when leaves are down, because the seed tell stands alone.

The white-vs-red group tell is redundant rather than single-point, which is what saves it. Bristle tips on leaves is the primary tell, but it is backed by kernel skin (fuzzy vs smooth), shell interior (woolly vs smooth) and the two-season vs one-season maturation showing two acorn sizes on one twig. That redundancy matters because entire-leaved red-group oaks (willow oak, shingle oak) carry only a tiny single terminal bristle a beginner can miss; the failure mode there is a longer leach and GI upset, which the entry states outright, not poisoning.

Required safety preparation is present and specific, not vague. Leaching is stated as mandatory ('Kernel only, and only after leaching'), with three quantified routes: cold steep over several days to a couple of weeks; meal rinsed six to twenty times until no longer astringent; or boiling in changes of water about fifteen minutes a change until the water stops running brown. It names the consequence of skipping it (gallotannins, abdominal pain, constipation then diarrhoea, per NC State) and states 'Never eat them raw or under-leached'. It also handles the non-lookalike hazards: discard nuts with weevil exit holes, dark discoloration or mould.

Months [7,8,9,10] = August-November, which is correct across the listed species (bur oak drops Aug-Nov, Q. alba Sept-Oct, Q. garryana late Aug-Nov, California valley oak Sept-Oct). No risk of sending someone out at the wrong time. Schema conformance is clean: all required fields present, months 0-indexed and in range, terrain and danger and caution values all valid.

NON-BLOCKING FLAW (regions under-inclusive, and self-contradictory). regions is ['midwest','northeast','southeast','west'], but the habitat text opens 'White-oak-group oaks reach every US region' and then explicitly names Q. gambelii and Q. arizonica in the Southwest and Q. muehlenbergii in the interior. Per src/data/seasonal-regional.ts, 'mountain' = MT/WY/CO/NM/AZ/UT/ID/NV (exactly Gambel and Arizona white oak country) and 'southcentral' = TX/OK (post oak, chinkapin oak, Q. fusiformis). Both are missing. I am not blocking on this because the error direction is safe: it hides the entry from Rockies and Texas users rather than sending anyone somewhere acorns are not. Recommended fix: set regions to ['all'].

NON-BLOCKING (terrain). terrain omits 'wetland' although the habitat specifically places Q. bicolor and swamp chestnut oak on 'bottomland and stream terraces'. Cosmetic inconsistency between the terrain tags and the entry's own prose.

NON-BLOCKING (suggested hardening, no field consequence as written). Three small things worth tightening on a later pass: (1) native buckeyes are rated 'toxic' while horse chestnut is 'deadly' - defensible, but California buckeye is severe enough that 'deadly' would be equally justifiable; it changes nothing in practice because caution is already 'expert' and the tell is identical for both. (2) The boil route omits the standard caveat never to let acorns cool or move them into cold water mid-leach, which sets the tannins - a palatability issue, not a safety one. (3) The cold-steep route gives a duration but no astringency endpoint of its own; the taste endpoint appears only in the meal route, though 'never under-leached' covers it.

NON-BLOCKING (editorial). The habitat actively steers beginners to 'street and park oaks' as 'the easiest gleaning' - correct as a horse chestnut warning, since that is where Aesculus is planted, but it carries no urban contamination caveat (roadside lead, herbicide, de-icing salt). Leaching does not remove lead. One sentence would close this.

approvedRevisedEntries.name: Black walnut
approvedRevisedEntries.habitat: Deep, well-drained, near-neutral bottomland and cove soils, plus fencerows, old-field edges, roadsides and yards, from New England west to eastern South Dakota and south to western Oklahoma, central Texas and northwest Florida. Those same river-bottom and cove sites are prime yellow buckeye ground - it wants the identical moist, deep, well-drained soil - and horse chestnut is a standard planted shade tree along the very roadsides and yards this entry sends you to, so expect Aesculus fruit underfoot in the same September woods. It will not tolerate poorly drained ground, so skip soggy bottoms; open-grown trees carry by far the heaviest crops. Widely planted well beyond this native range.
approvedRevisedEntries.indicator: An open-crowned tree with dark, diamond-furrowed bark standing over conspicuously bare ground - juglone from its roots suppresses plants under the dripline.
approvedRevisedEntries.parts: Kernel only. Identify the tree before you pick anything up: alternate, pinnately compound leaves one to two feet long with 15-23 leaflets, dark diamond-furrowed bark, and a fleshy green husk holding exactly one rock-hard, deeply grooved nut - never the opposite, palmate leaves and three-valved capsule of a buckeye. Cut the first fruit of the day through with a knife as a positive check: black walnut is thick fibrous green flesh whose juice stains the blade and your fingers yellow-brown within minutes, wrapped around a single shell the knife cannot enter, while a buckeye is a thin leathery rind over one to three smooth, shell-less seeds the blade slices straight through into solid ivory. The husk is not food: its juice stains skin, clothing and concrete brown for weeks and can irritate skin, so wear rubber gloves. Only once the tree is confirmed does ripeness matter - gather when the green husk dents under thumb pressure, then hull the same day, because a two-week delay in husk removal turns kernels black and rancid. The dent test is a ripeness test and nothing more: a green buckeye capsule dents under thumb pressure too, so it can never stand in for identification. Wash the nuts, throw out any that are mouldy or whose shells are cracked or fissured, then cure them in a single layer one nut deep in a cool, dry, ventilated spot out of direct sun for two to three weeks before cracking. Keep shelled kernels in the fridge or freezer; the oil goes rancid quickly.

lookalikes.name: Buckeyes and horse chestnut (Aesculus flava, A. glabra, A. hippocastanum, A. pavia)
lookalikes.tell: Habitat and calendar put this one directly under your feet: yellow buckeye (A. flava) grows in the same river bottoms, coves and moist north slopes as black walnut and drops a smooth, round, leathery capsule 1.5-2 in across - the same size and silhouette as a green walnut hull; Ohio buckeye (A. glabra) fruits September-October in the same rich valley, ravine and low-woods edge; and horse chestnut is a standard yard and street planting. Thumb pressure will not separate them - a green Aesculus capsule dents too - so cut the fruit through. Black walnut is thick fibrous green flesh, sharply aromatic, whose juice stains the blade and your fingers yellow-brown within minutes, around one rock-hard, deeply corrugated shell the knife cannot enter. Aesculus is a thin leathery rind peeling off one to three smooth, shell-less seeds - glossy mahogany when ripe, pale ivory when green, each with one large pale scar - that the blade cuts straight into as solid ivory, with no stain and no smell. A drying Aesculus capsule shows three sutures and splits into three valves; a walnut husk is fleshy and never splits. Overhead the difference is absolute: Aesculus leaves are opposite and palmate, five to seven leaflets radiating from one point; walnut leaves are alternate and pinnate, 15-23 leaflets along a stalk one to two feet long. NC State Extension rates both A. flava and A. hippocastanum Poison Severity: High, saying of yellow buckeye that it can cause death in humans, livestock and pets and of horse chestnut that it is highly toxic and may be fatal if eaten; poison centres record severe poisoning - weakness, twitching, paralysis, collapse, airway swelling - after only one to four seeds, with children the usual casualties. No Aesculus seed is edible by any preparation, and no amount of leaching makes one safe.

lookalikes.name: Osage orange (Maclura pomifera)
lookalikes.tell: Osage orange fruit is a 4-5 inch yellow-green ball with a wrinkled, brainlike surface that bleeds sticky white latex (a skin irritant) when cut; its leaves are simple, glossy and smooth-edged and its twigs carry straight half-inch thorns. Black walnut fruit is a smooth green sphere about 1.5-2.5 inches across holding one hard nut, on a thornless tree with pinnately compound leaves.

approvedRevisedEntries.harvest: Pick nuts up off the ground within a few days of the drop, never from the tree. Ask permission for yard trees, and skip trees on sprayed lawns, sprayed rights-of-way and busy road shoulders. Spread your take across several heavy-bearing yard or roadside trees rather than stripping one isolated woodland tree, whose crop is winter mast for squirrels, deer and turkey. Discard any nut that overwintered on the ground, shows mould, or has a cracked or fissured shell: Penicillium crustosum growing on fallen walnuts produces the tremorgenic mycotoxin penitrem A, documented in dog poisonings and in one adult man who ate about eight mouldy kernels and developed tremors, incoordination and confusion within 12 hours. Anyone with a tree-nut allergy should not eat these at all - walnut is a major food allergen and anaphylaxis is the one hazard here that genuinely kills. Oblong, sticky-hairy fruits are butternut (Juglans cinerea): also edible, but leave them, as the species is collapsing from butternut canker.

approvedRevisedNotes.name: Black walnut
reasons: SCHEMA: clean. All fields present and correctly typed against src/data/foraging.ts. caution='expert' is justified (a 'deadly' lookalike exists). lookalikes[].danger values are in-enum. terrain values (woodland/edge/disturbed) are in-enum and match the prose; wetland is correctly EXCLUDED because the habitat explicitly says the tree will not tolerate poorly drained ground.

MONTHS: correctly 0-indexed, not a 1-indexed slip. [8,9,10] resolves to Sep/Oct/Nov, which matches the entry's own prose ('September-October ripening', 'the same September woods') plus a southern tail. Consistent with corpus practice — the approved Chestnut entry uses [7,8,9,10] for the same Sept-Oct core with tails at both ends.

DEADLY LOOKALIKE: Aesculus is present, correctly tiered 'deadly', and handled better than the usual published treatment. Critically, the entry names FOUR species (A. flava, A. glabra, A. hippocastanum, A. pavia) rather than only horse chestnut, and it co-locates them honestly: yellow buckeye shares the identical river-bottom/cove soil, Ohio buckeye fruits Sept-Oct in the same rich valleys, and horse chestnut is a standard yard/street planting on the very roadsides the entry sends you to. It does not pretend the two don't overlap.

TELL QUALITY: the discriminator is a cut test that is absolute, in-season, and works on the fruit as found on the ground — walnut is thick fibrous flesh around one rock-hard corrugated shell the knife CANNOT enter, staining blade and fingers yellow-brown; Aesculus is a thin rind over 1-3 smooth shell-less seeds the blade slices straight through into solid ivory, no stain, no smell. Backed by three more independent filters: leaf arrangement overhead (alternate pinnate 15-23 leaflets vs opposite palmate 5-7), capsule dehiscence (Aesculus splits into 3 valves, walnut husk never splits), and the hulling step itself, which a buckeye physically cannot survive since it has no shell. Four layers is more than a beginner needs.

BEST FEATURE — the anti-tell: the entry explicitly demotes the ripeness test so it cannot be mistaken for an ID test ('The dent test is a ripeness test and nothing more: a green buckeye capsule dents under thumb pressure too, so it can never stand in for identification'), and orders the steps so identification precedes ripeness. This closes a real and specific failure mode that most walnut write-ups leave wide open.

SAFETY PREP: complete. Husk is declared not-food with rubber gloves specified for the staining/irritant juice; hull same day (2-week delay blackens and turns kernels rancid); discard mouldy, cracked or fissured shells; cure single-layer 2-3 weeks; refrigerate/freeze kernels for rancidity. The mould hazard is specific rather than hand-waved — Penicillium crustosum, penitrem A, with both the dog and the adult-human case (~8 mouldy kernels, tremors/incoordination/confusion within 12 hours) cited to PMIDs. Tree-nut anaphylaxis is flagged as the hazard that actually kills. Contamination (sprayed lawns, rights-of-way, road shoulders) and permission for yard trees are covered.

SOURCES: 16 citations, all extension/agency/peer-reviewed (USDA FS Silvics, NC State Plant Toolbox, Iowa State, Illinois, Missouri IPM, Clemson, MDC, NCPC, two PubMed entries, MedlinePlus). Quoted material is attributed accurately. Notably it cites Silvics for yellow buckeye specifically to substantiate the shared-habitat claim rather than asserting it.

FIX (non-blocking, accuracy): regions omits 'southcentral' while the entry's own habitat text extends the range to 'western Oklahoma, central Texas'. A Texas or Oklahoma forager will never be shown this entry. Under-inclusion is not a safety risk, and adding southcentral needs no new lookalikes (A. glabra and A. pavia already cover Texas/Ohio buckeye), so this is a one-word fix. Corpus precedent supports it — Chestnut lists southcentral for a weaker claim ('eastern Oklahoma and east Texas').

FIX (non-blocking, wording): 'Cut the first fruit of the day through with a knife' should be 'the first fruit under each tree'. Per-day is the wrong cadence for an entry that itself stresses walnut and yellow buckeye standing in the same bottomland — a forager who moves to a second tree should re-cut. The adjacent 'Identify the tree before you pick anything up' already implies per-tree, so this is only a tightening.

CONSIDER (non-blocking): tung tree (Vernicia fordii) is toxic, naturalized across the Gulf South including the northwest Florida corner of the stated range, and drops a fleshy green ~2 in autumn fruit. The entry's existing protocol already catches it (simple heart-shaped leaves vs pinnate; 3-7 seeds vs one on the cut), so this is completeness, not a gap.

COSMETIC: the buckeye cut-test description is repeated near-verbatim between `parts` and the lookalike `tell` — verbose, though the approved corpus is comparably verbose and the redundancy is on the safety-critical step, which is the right place for it. Separately, `indicator` slightly overstates juglone: bare ground under the dripline is real but variable (turf grass tolerates juglone fine), so 'conspicuously bare' may not read true on a mown yard tree. Harmless — the indicator is a locating hint and is never load-bearing for the walnut/buckeye call.

NOTED, NO CHANGE WANTED: 'no amount of leaching makes one safe' is stricter than the ethnobotanical record (some groups did leach A. californica). Weakening it would be a safety regression for a beginner audience. Leave it as written.

VERDICT: approve. A beginner following this in order — ID the tree by leaves, cut one fruit, hull, discard mouldy/cracked, cure, refrigerate — cannot reach a buckeye, and is warned about the two hazards that actually put people in hospital (mould neurotoxin and nut allergy). Not a duplicate; no Juglans entry exists in approved.json or src/data/foraging-species.ts. The two FIX items are worth applying before publish but neither is a safety blocker.
